webTitle: US military has no plans to send troops to midterm polling sites, Dan Caine says

fields.headline: US military has no plans to send troops to midterm polling sites, Dan Caine says
fields.trailText: Letter from chair of joint chiefs of staff addresses concerns over Trump officials using military to interfere with vote
fields.bodyText: The highest‑ranking US military officer says there are no plans to deploy troops to polling places during the November midterm elections – responding to Senator Elissa Slotkin’s request for information amid concerns about whether the Trump administration might send service members to election sites. In a letter obtained by the Guardian, first reported by the Associated Press, Gen Dan Caine, chair of the joint chiefs of staff, told Slotkin “the Joint Force has no plans to send Federal military personnel or Federalized members of the National Guard to polling places during the 2026 elections”. He added that there were also “no plans to use such personnel to seize ballots, voting machines, or other election‑related material”. Slotkin – a Democrat who serves on the Senate armed services and homeland security committees – sought confirmation from Caine and the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, after Donald Trump urged Republicans to “nationalize” elections and said he had not ruled out sending guard members or immigration enforcement agents to the polls. In his letter, Caine added: “I have neither received nor anticipate receiving any unlawful order concerning the role of the Joint Force in the upcoming November 2026 midterm elections.” Slotkin’s office had not yet received a reply from Hegseth, said Sonja Thrasher, her press secretary. The senator had asked both men to respond by 28 August. Anxiety among Democrats that the Trump administration could try to meddle in the midterm elections has grown, particularly after the president deployed federal agents in Democratic-led states over the objections of local leaders. Slotkin told the AP earlier in August that Trump had been laying the groundwork to claim the elections were stolen. She noted that Trump contemplated using the military to seize voting machines after his loss in 2020 and had deployed the national guard to cities against the wishes of Democratic leaders. He also deployed active-duty marines to Los Angeles during his immigration crackdown in 2025. Federal law prohibits the deployment of armed federal forces to election locations unless “necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States”. If any element of the military were to get involved, it would probably be the national guard under state control. Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, denied in a Vanity Fair interview last year that Trump would use the military to suppress voting in the midterms. The Pentagon did not immediately respond to an email from the Guardian asking for the status of Hegseth’s response to Slotkin. Slotkin asked Hegseth during an April congressional hearing if he would follow orders to seize ballots. Hegseth called the question a “gotcha hypothetical”, but said: “I’ve never been ordered to do anything illegal, and I won’t.” In 2020, Gen Mark Milley, then chair of the joint chiefs of staff, responded to a similar letter from Slotkin, a congresswoman at the time. “I believe deeply in the principle of an apolitical U.S. military,” Milley wrote. “In the event of a dispute over some aspect of the elections, by law U.S. courts and the U.S. Congress are required to resolve any disputes, not the U.S. military.”

webTitle: Trump attacks datacenter backlash, claiming communities pushing back risk becoming ‘backwards and poor’

fields.headline: Trump attacks datacenter backlash, claiming communities pushing back risk becoming ‘backwards and poor’
fields.trailText: Three-quarters of Americans said in a recent poll that they oppose datacenters being built next to their homes
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump has criticized communities pushing back against datacenter projects across the US amid a growing backlash, warning those that reject them risk becoming “backwards and poor”. As controversy surrounding local datacenter plans continues to swirl around election campaigns nationwide ahead of November’s midterm elections, the US president declared Americans “will only have yourselves to blame” if they are canceled. Bipartisan opposition to datacenter expansion has intensified across the US, particularly in states with ample land, low-cost power and generous tax incentives, as local communities raise concerns over environmental impacts, soaring utility costs and noise pollution. According to a recent poll, three-quarters of Americans said they would oppose a datacenter being built next to their homes, while more than six in 10 Americans said they would strongly oppose such a proposal. In a Truth Social post on Monday, Trump wrote: “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign. “The good news is that there are plenty of other places that want them. If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame. China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement. Actually, they can’t believe it is happening!” Responding to Trump’s statement on Monday, JD Vance told reporters that datacenters were an “important part of the AI economy”, adding: “When people build them, they have to build the power plants along with the datacenters. I think probably 99% of the backlash to datacenters has come in areas where building a datacenter means higher utility and higher electricity for the people on the ground. “I think what these companies have to do is take advantage of some of the federal deregulatory efforts that we’ve undertaken,” the US vice-president added. “If you build a datacenter, you should be putting power back into the grid, not taking it out. And if that is happening, I don’t think the datacenters are that controversial. It’s when the utility bills get so much higher that’s when it’s a real problem.” However, several users replied to Trump’s post on his own Truth Social platform, voicing their concerns about datacenters. “Mr. President: Think about farm land and about water resources, and a man as intelligent as you will see that the absolute position you are taking is flawed,” one user wrote. “What use is being rich if you cannot get access to water and food?” As opposition to datacenters grows, the research group Data Center Watch found that grassroots groups blocked or delayed at least 75 datacenter projects worth approximately $130bn in the first three months of 2026. Monterey Park, a small city east of Los Angeles, is among the local communities that have pushed back against datacenters and won. Other communities successful in their resistance include Prince William county, Virginia, as well as Wake county, North Carolina. Environmental groups have also weighed in, with a coalition of more than 230 organizations urging members of Congress last year to halt the development of new datacenters amid the climate crisis, worsening droughts in already water-stressed areas, and rising electricity bills.

webTitle: James Clyburn says supporting Clarence Thomas for supreme court ‘was mistake’

fields.headline: James Clyburn says supporting Clarence Thomas for supreme court ‘was mistake’
fields.trailText: Congressman says Thomas abandoned his principles to become an extremist, hard-right member of bench
fields.bodyText: The senior Democratic congressman James Clyburn said his decision to support Clarence Thomas for a US supreme court seat “was a mistake” and called for the expansion of the nation’s highest legal panel to 13 justices. Clyburn, of South Carolina, spoke up for Thomas at his fiery 1991 confirmation hearings, calling him “a personal and professional friend” who would use their shared experiences lifting minorities and advancing civil rights to become a respected and accomplished jurist. Instead, Clyburn told NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday, Thomas abandoned his principles to become an extremist, hard-right member of a bench that has delivered some stunning legal reversals in recent years, including the overturning of federal protections for abortion and ending affirmative action in higher education. Asked by host Kristen Welker if he regretted standing up for Thomas, Clyburn replied: “I have made mistakes in my life, and that’s one that I made. And I will own up to that mistake. “I had no idea that Clarence Thomas would rebel the way he has against his own background and experiences. He was raised by his grandfather, and he has shown very little sensitivity to the environment his grandfather grew up down in Pin Point, Georgia.” Before joining Congress in 1993, Clyburn was South Carolina’s human affairs commissioner for 18 years beginning in 1974. He said Thomas’s tenure as chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission from 1982 until 1990, a time in which it vigorously pursued anti-discrimination legal actions, had assured him that Thomas “believed in precedents, the law”. He told Welker: “I had faith and confidence in the fact that his background and experiences would instruct him in his professionalism, especially sitting on the bench. I thought, sure, that he would be here upholding those precedents set down in 1954 in the Brown v Board of Education decision” that declared racial segregation in public schools was illegal. But Thomas, whose later years on the bench have been mired in allegations of corruption, turned his back on civil rights, Clyburn suggested, notably in the 2024 decision on ideological grounds that ruled affirmative action in college admissions unconstitutional. “That was a mistake on my part,” Clyburn said of his past support for Thomas. “And I own up to it.” Clyburn spoke as the prospect of increasing the number of US supreme court justices, a popular rallying cry for sections of the Democratic party as it attempts to retake the House in November’s midterms, returned to public discourse. Former Democratic vice-president Kamala Harris in July called for the expansion of the bench from nine to 13, a proposal Clyburn said he would support. “Thirteen is a pretty good number,” he said. “A baker’s dozen would be a good number to have on the court. “And I would hope we would get people on the court who will follow the constitutional underpinnings of this great nation of ours. I had hoped that Clarence Thomas would follow the underpinnings of that constitution of ours, but he has not done so. “In fact, he’s decided to go all the way from an angry leftist, to a very angry rightist.” Clyburn, however, said Democrats’ immediate priorities after November should not be either supreme court expansion or impeachment of Donald Trump for what would be a third time across his two presidencies. “If the Democrats were to take back the House, and I feel confident that we will, our first order of business ought to be developing an accessible and affordable campaign effort that will yield what I will call making this country, its greatness, accessible and affordable for all of its citizens,” he said.

webTitle: A pediatrician is running for Senate. Can doctors change the political debate over health and science?

fields.headline: A pediatrician is running for Senate. Can doctors change the political debate over health and science?
fields.trailText: After Lindsey Graham’s death, Democrat Annie Andrews finds herself in a closely watched race as she seeks to flip his Republican seat
fields.bodyText: Annie Andrews was a dark horse Democrat challenging a five-term Republican in the US Senate when 314 Action, a political action fund devoted to electing scientists and doctors, first backed her. Now, after the unexpected death of Senator Lindsey Graham, Andrews finds herself in a closely watched race. Donald Trump persuaded South Carolina voters last week to select Graham’s sister, Darline, as the new Republican candidate. They will face off in November in an election still heavily favored to keep the seat in Republican hands in the conservative state. Andrews, a pediatrician for 20 years, has made public health and science a central part of her campaign, highlighting the importance of vaccines as measles spread through South Carolina – and so have the other candidates supported by 314 Action. Last year, 314 laid out an ambitious goal: elect at least 100 doctors to state and federal office by 2030. The group had an initial fundraising target of $25m, which it reached in August, to help establish Democratic doctors in state legislatures, governorships, and federal offices – “building that pipeline of talent to higher office”, said Shaughnessy Naughton, president of 314 Action. Headlines in 2026 have been dominated by outbreaks of infectious diseases and foodborne illnesses, the biggest cuts to Medicaid in its history, the gutting of scientific research, immigration raids in hospitals, and more, making health and science salient issues in the US midterm elections. Doctors and experts are “on the frontlines of this”, Andrews said. “I don’t think there’s ever been a more important time to elect scientists and medical doctors to all levels of our government.” In the 2018 midterm elections, record numbers of people – nearly 200 – with backgrounds in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (Stem) ran for House and Senate seats. But only about 12% of the candidates won, according to research by Matthew Motta, assistant professor at Boston University’s School of Public Health. “So to say that you want to get 100 physicians to not just run but to actually be elected to public office is quite a tall order,” he said. Endorsement and financial support from 314 Action do increase the likelihood that Stem candidates will win, according to his research. But the goal of 100 wins in the next four years is ambitious, Motta said. In fact, candidates with Stem backgrounds were less likely to win than non-Stem peers in 2018, according to an analysis co-authored by Meredith Conroy, political science professor at California State University, San Bernardino. They probably didn’t lose because of their science background, Conroy said, adding: “I just don’t think it was a salient enough identity at the time to suggest it made or broke their campaign.” But recent events are changing that, making health and science a top-of-mind concern for voters, Conroy and Motta pointed out. “It’s really important then, if we want to defend science from politicized attacks on its daily operation, that those who actually do science and who do medicine are elected to Congress,” Motta said. State-level leadership on health will also be key as national health agencies falter and as states consider restrictive laws on issues like vaccination and reproductive health, Motta said. Josh Green, the governor of Hawaii and an emergency physician, is the only doctor-governor in the United States right now. But he wants to feel less alone. “We want to create a bench of people” who are better-qualified and could be appointed to positions like these, Green said. He is mentoring candidates through 314 on how to engage with constituents and “how to message in a way that political people have to master”. There are 20 physicians in the House and Senate right now, but only six of the House representatives are Democrats, and there are no Democratic doctors in the Senate. Running for office takes deep pockets, which means doctors who are already wealthy – a group that tends to skew conservative – are more likely to be elected. Some of these doctors, like Rand Paul, have contributed to misinformation on vaccines and other health issues. That partisan divide is increasingly evident when it comes to health, Motta noted: “Just because somebody has a scientific background does not necessarily mean that they’re going to fight for science.” Yet electing more physicians could help repair trust in science, Naughton said, as “most people do trust their physicians and they bring a lot of credibility.” Doctor-politicians aren’t just important for opposing harmful laws or misinformation, Naughton added. They also have a fact-based approach to problem solving. Scientists and doctors frequently go into debt for their education, making it difficult for them to leave their fields for politics, Green pointed out. He was only able to do it because he qualified for student loan forgiveness through the National Health Service Corps. “Had I had $300,000 or $400,000 of debt, like a lot of my colleagues from medical school, I could never have run for the state house. There’s no way,” he said. “If we can seed their campaigns with enough money to get off the ground,” Green said of new candidates, “they’ll stand a chance.” When Barbara Bollier, an anesthesiologist and a Republican-turned-Democratic state lawmaker in Kansas, decided to run for the Senate in 2020, she knew the odds were long. Kansas hadn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. Even though Bollier lost that race, she still feels victorious. “I moved the ball down the field,” she said. She received more votes than any Democrat in the history of the state, she said, and when the next big health issue arose in Kansas, the state shocked the country by voting to protect abortion rights. There’s a persistent belief that medicine and science are above politics, Naughton said, pointing out “that approach has failed us … We need folks to go beyond just signing polite letters and waiting to be tapped as scientific advisers, and actually step up and claim the seat at the table.” And the stakes are high: “The hard truth of it is, people are going to die if we don’t follow science,” Green said. Running for office “was not something I ever, in a million years, thought I would be doing with my life”, Andrews said. At the age of four, she told her preschool teacher she would be a doctor one day, and she never wavered from that plan. But “it became clear to me that the most effective and efficient way to solve the problems my patients and their families were facing was through politics, by changing who actually has the power, by electing people who inherently care about America’s children,” she said. It would take decades to counter the misinformation and damage from officials currently in power, Andrews said. But she is in it for the long haul. “I’m just so happy to be a part of this movement of physicians all across the country raising their hands, stepping up to run for office,” she said.

webTitle: AI is hurting US politics. Here’s how candidates could use it for good | Bruce Schneier and Nathan E Sanders

fields.headline: AI is hurting US politics. Here’s how candidates could use it for good
fields.trailText: The technology can help candidates listen more deeply to voters, as examples from Japan and Scotland show
fields.bodyText: There are plenty of signs that AI will make all of our experiences of the US midterm elections worse. Voters have anxiety about AI’s impacts on the country. Politicos are using AI deepfakes to spread lies. The White House is posting slopaganda. Meanwhile, candidates are missing a real opportunity to use AI to make campaigning better. The technology can help candidates listen more deeply to voters’ concerns, engage constituents more inclusively, and formulate policy platforms that are more responsive to our input. There are vanishingly few examples of this in US politics, but groups in Japan, Scotland and the US’s own academic and private institutions show how that could change. The problem with American campaigns’ current use of AI is that it’s not very different from the web ads of 30 years ago, or television ads before that: they are all about inundating voters with the candidate’s message. This one-to-many broadcasting is an uninspiring way to campaign, but not the only way. AI can help candidates connect one-to-one with as many people as possible. Or it can facilitate many-to-many connections, engaging voters in deliberation about issues at scale. One of the most promising applications of AI being developed by pro-democracy innovators around the world is broad listening. These tools can collect public input in a format much richer than checkboxes on a survey form. For example, the newly founded Japanese political party Team Mirai has built a foundation for eliciting public input from voters at scale, in depth, and across the breadth of legislative policy issues. It has developed an AI interviewer to cultivate constituent input on policy. Through extended conversations with this chatbot, voters explore and share their perspectives on specific policy issues. And the party has scaled this across a wide array of policy issues by integrating this functionality with an AI-powered portal for exploring bills. Team Mirai describes itself as a “utility party”, developing tools for any Japanese political party to use to connect with voters. You might question whether Americans would willingly talk to a political AI. So far, Japanese voters have exchanged more than 300,000 messages across 16,000 AI interviews. Team Mirai grew adoption by providing a real incentive to engage: that talking to their AI interviewer does more than just posting on a platform such as Twitter/X or, equivalently, shouting into a void. Users see evidence that the party is actually listening and might take action on their behalf. Team Mirai party members have directly cited AI interviews from constituents during legislative committee hearings, published a synthesis of that input back for voters, and even amended their policy platform based on user input. The party has rapidly risen to win 12 seats in the Diet, and is explicitly following in the footsteps of the civic hackers in Taiwan’s “gov zero” movement, who won political influence in their fight for transparency. Other civic technologists are developing AI tools for scaling many-to-many conversations. CrownShy, a company funded in part by the Scottish government, is building a platform to bring the Platonic ideal of the town hall debate into the digital age. Their Comhairle tool integrates AI interviewing tools like the ones described above with software for synthesizing diverse viewpoints, holding virtual assemblies, and sharing video testimonials to help legislatures – or campaigners – organize digital consultations of their constituents en masse. One thing the AI-powered software of Team Mirai and CrownShy have in common is that they are open-source, meant for anyone to use. Even though they are projects funded by political parties – the upstart party in Japan and the ruling party in Scotland – they are built to make democratic processes better, not necessarily for partisan political advantage. For interested candidates, there is a wealth of tools available, many of them US-grown. The Stanford-affiliated deliberation.io uses AI to facilitate structured dialogues among thousands of participants and has been piloted for public listening sessions by the city of Washington DC. The MIT-affiliated Cortico project provides tools that surface under-heard community perspectives from recorded conversations, and is now organizing listening sessions at libraries across the country. The US non-profit-built Talk to the City uses AI to analyze large datasets of stakeholder input. The US startup Remesh has a commercial offering that uses AI to generate recommendations from dialogue, which has been tested in policy development scenarios. There is a long and proud tradition of this sort of “civic technology” in the United States. Two decades ago, the spirit of innovation to develop software for better politics and civic engagement was so strong in organizations like Code for America and the Obama 2008 campaign that Congress funded a new executive agency to bring these ideas to government: the US Digital Service. (The Trump administration repurposed the USDS to become the US Doge Service in 2025.) One signal that candidates and political parties may start adopting these kinds of tools came this spring from Higher Ground Labs. The Democratic-aligned campaign tech investment firm launched a new fund targeting, in part, “AI-Native Campaign Systems” and “community-Led Messaging Platforms that surface authentic, bottom-up insights from real conversations”. AI is a multifaceted issue that deserves to be on the table in the midterms. So far, the powerful force of polarization in US politics seems to be separating the parties into the AI skeptics versus the AI boosters. We urge both voters and politicians to separate the technology of AI from its profiteers. We want big tech money out of politics, holding the AI companies accountable for the harm their models cause, taxing their revenues, and maybe even nationalizing them if the AI bubble bursts. But we also think congressional candidates in the US midterms seeking authentic connection with voters, and seeking to differentiate themselves from their opponents, should be looking to use AI responsibly in their campaigning. The broad listening and deliberation tools pioneered by others around the world could make US politics more transparent, responsive and community-driven. The impact of AI on campaigning doesn’t have to be all bad. Bruce Schneier is a security technologist who teaches at the Harvard Kennedy School and the University of Toronto’s Munk School of Global Affairs & Public Policy Nathan E Sanders is a data scientist affiliated with the Berkman Klein Center of Harvard University and co-author, with Bruce Schneier, of the book Rewiring Democracy: How AI Will Transform Our Politics, Government, and Citizenship • This article was amended on 31 August 2026. An earlier version incorrectly described CrownShy as a non-profit.
